The observed decline stems primarily from outdated redlining-era policies that artificially suppressed investment and credit access in minority communities, creating a cycle of under-investment.
Concurrently, a lack of adequate public infrastructure and service access has exacerbated safety concerns, which negatively impacts property valuations regardless of active crime rates.
Reliance on simplistic statistical correlations regarding crime and demographics ignores the historical and systemic financial barriers that isolated these neighborhoods long before recent data emerged.
Therefore, addressing this issue requires targeted community reinvestment strategies rather than punitive measures that implicitly blame resident demographics.
